lessons.title: Setting up your environment (Beginner)
lessons.content:
Welcome to VEX Programming!

This guide will help you install VS Code and the VEX Extension on your laptop. If you have any questions, please ask Dan!

Why Programming Matters

Even if your robot is amazing, bad programming will hold your team back. Good programming can be the difference between winning and losing. You will decide your fate!

What is VEX Code?

VEX code is very similar to C++, but has minor differences in syntax. It's very intuitive! Any individual can learn VEX code without prior knowledge and utilize it to its fullest potential.

* Any prior knowledge in another programming language can be beneficial!

What is Visual Studio (VS) Code?

Visual Studio Code is an IDE (integrated development environment), software that allows people to easily program.

There are many IDEs (Pycharm, IntelliJ, etc), each with unique purposes. Some, like VS Code, specialize in specific coding languages like C++.

However, VS Code also allows you to add "extensions" that allow you to code in other languages (like VEX V5!)

Installation Steps

There are three steps to installation:

  1. Installing Visual Studio Code
  2. Installing VEX's VS Extension
  3. Installing Python/C++ Extensions

Step 1: Install Visual Studio Code

Go to code.visualstudio.com/download and download VS Code for your operating system (Windows or Mac).

Once installed, open VS Code. It should look something like this:

VS Code has a good welcome guide that you can follow. If you don't see it, go to Help → Welcome.

Step 2: Install VEX Robotics Extension

Click on the Extensions icon in the left sidebar (it looks like 4 squares).

Type "VEX Robotics" in the search bar and click on the first option. Hit Install!

You have now downloaded the V5 Extension! Whenever you want to code in VEX, just click on the VEX icon in the sidebar and select one of the project actions.

Step 3: Install C++/Python Extensions

Like "VEX Robotics", search up C++/C# and Python in the Extensions marketplace and install both! (It's important)

Congrats!

Yay! You did it! Now you're ready to start programming your robot.

Continue to the next lessons to learn the basics of VEX programming.

quiz.question: What is VS Code an example of?
quiz.explanation: VS Code is an IDE — software for writing and managing code. With the VEX extension it can program V5 robots. VEX code itself is very similar to C++.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.0: Basics of Programming
lessons.content:
In this module

You will learn:

  • What VEX code is
  • Learn the basics of programming

Variable Types

Integer (int)Double (double)String (string)Boolean (bool)
Stores variables (whole numbers), without decimal, such as 123 or -123Stores floating point numbers, with decimals, such as 10.21 or -122.12Stores text such as "VEX is great!" String values are surrounded by double quotes.Stores values with two states: true or false

If Statements

Logical Conditions

  • Less than: a < b
  • Less than or equal to: a <= b
  • Greater than: a > b
  • Greater than or equal to: a >= b
  • Equal to: a == b
  • Not Equal to: a != b

Use the if statement to specify a block of code to be executed, if a specified condition is true.

if (condition) {
  // block of code to be executed if the condition is true
}

If... else... Statements

Use "else" to specify a block of code to be executed, if the same condition is false.

if (condition) {
  // block of code to be executed if the condition is true
} else {
  // block of code to be executed if the condition is false
}

Basic Motor, Controller, etc. Commands

.spin().stop().setVelocity()
To spin motors forward or reverse.
motorname.spin(forward) or motorname.spin(reverse)		Stops motors from moving.
motorname.stop(brake)		Sets speed of motors, with two parameters, speed and unit.
motorname.setVelocity(80, percent)
.position().set()Bonus: .print()
Used to find position of joystick on controller.
Controller.Axis4.position()		Used in pneumatics to set the value of the piston to be true or false.
piston.set(false) or piston.set(true)		To print information on the Screen of the Brain.
Brain.Screen.print(motor.temperature());

Creating a Competition Template

VEX Extension → New Project → V5 → C/C++ → V5 Competition Template Project

Why not Python? VEX Programmers globally use C++ more (because VEX was originally made with it)

Understanding the main.cpp file

All the code that you will create will be placed in the main.cpp file. Don't worry about coding in any other file unless you know how to navigate it.

The competition template is separated into different functions. This allows you to create separate code for a game's autonomous period and driver control period.

In the future, you'll likely write some code for auton. For now, let's try and get a motor moving based on user input by writing code in the usercontrol() function.

Define Electronics

First, let's define our electronics: the brain, controller, and motor. Each of these components are types of objects, just like ints and Strings.

Remember, to create an object, syntax looks like this:

(component name)(name provided);

OR

(component name)(name provided) = (component name)(parameters);

Define Brain

On the line highlighted, define a brain by typing:

brain Brain;

Define Controller

Now that you've defined a brain, try doing the same for the controller. Note that the component name for a controller is controller. The name you provide is up to you, but most people just name it Controller1 by convention.

controller Controller1;

Define Motor

Motors require specific parameters. There are actually 4 different parameters to define motors:

  • PORTS parameter - tells the code which port is assigned to which motor (Eg. Port 1 on the brain will send signals for the left wheel)
  • ratio18_1 - gear setting for different motor colors:
    • Green motors uses ratio18_1 (default)
    • Red motors use ratio6_1
    • Blue motors use ratio36_1
  • Reverse - a boolean, can reverse the way a motor spins by default. False by default.
motor leftWheel = motor(PORT1);

Coding Motors!

Now that we've defined our electronics, let's get a motor spinning! We'll be typing in the usercontrol() function under the while loop.

The while loop will constantly update your robot's electronics. We're going to add an if statement to move a motor when an input (eg. if we tilt a joystick) is true.

Finding positions of joysticks

.position() syntax/parameters:

(Controller name).(Axis #).position()

Axis Numbers:

  • X-axis right joystick = Axis 1
  • Y-axis right joystick = Axis 2
  • Y-axis left joystick = Axis 3
  • X-axis left joystick = Axis 4

Position values follow a coordinate plane. On the left/right axis, all the way left = -1, all the way right = 1. All the way down = -1, all the way up = 1.

Motor Spin Code

if (Controller1.Axis1.position() > 0) {
  leftWheel.spin(forward);
}

Adding Stop Functionality

At the current procedure, once the motor starts spinning, it will never stop. To fix this, we need an else statement to stop the motor.

if (Controller1.Axis1.position() > 0) {
  leftWheel.spin(forward);
} else {
  leftWheel.stop();
}

Making Your Code Run!

Downloading Code

To download code on to your robot, you must connect your computer to a controller or brain (preferably the former).

  1. Connect computer to your controller
  2. Make sure controller is connected to active brain (turned on)
  3. Press buttons and go
  4. Also, to test code: don't hit the run button. Run it on your brain.

Running Your Code

Use your controller and follow the following instructions. Use the A button to confirm and arrow keys to switch between selections.

Go to Programs → (Project Name) → Run Code

Then you can start testing!

Documenting Code

Good code documentation is important! Here's an example of good vs bad documentation:

Warning!

If you're completely new to code and are running through this self-guided, it is a lot better to come ask Dan Honda for help regarding this section.

quiz.question: Which variable type stores a value that is either true or false?
quiz.explanation: A bool (boolean) holds exactly two states: true or false. int stores whole numbers, double stores decimals, and string stores text.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.0: Coding a Drivebase
lessons.content:
In this module

You should've learned:

  • Module 0: Installation Guide
  • Module 1: Programming Introduction

You will learn:

  • How to initialize a tank drive
  • How to code a tank drivebase

Table of Contents

  1. Initializing a tank drive
  2. Review: Motor Coding
  3. Coding your drivebase

Section 1: Initializing a Tank Drive

Initializing Our Variables

Here is a list of the devices we will need to initialize:

  • Brain
  • Controller
  • 4 motors (to control wheels of drivebase)
  • Motor groups (recommended)

Initializing your Motors

In Module 1.0, you learned about how to initialize motors, now we will need to define 4 of them:

Consider the names of the motors, you want to be able to clearly identify which motor you're spinning.

Make sure the ports of each motor is different.

For example:

Initializing your Motors (IMPORTANT)

You need to make sure forward is actually forward. From Module 1.1, we learned that motors rotate following the arrow on the back of the motor.

Pick a side of your robot to be forward. Now you need to reverse the motors whose red arrows are going the opposite direction to the "forward direction", using your code.

Most robots will have both motors on the right moving in the opposite direction. To account for this take a look at the following code:

** Make sure you reverse the motors on YOUR robot. Check in with leadership if you're confused.

Setting true means reverse is ON. Set motors you want to reverse to true.

Initializing Motor Groups

In a tank drive, both of your left wheels AND both of your right wheels will always be spinning in the same direction. Instead of coding each individual motor to spin every time, you can code a motor group to spin.

Here is the structure of creating a motor group:

motor_group (Group name)((name of motor 1), (name of motor 2), ...)

** You can add any number of motors in the brackets

For example:

Initializing your Brain & Controller

This should be a review from Module 1.0. Make sure you know where to initialize your devices:

If you have any questions about how we initialized these electronics, refer to the 1.0 slides.

Initializing Motor Groups (cont.)

We need to create 2 motor groups, one for your left wheels and one for your right wheels. This is what it should look like:

Initialization Final

This is what your initialization should look like:

Section 2: Motor Coding Review

Spinning a Motor Review

Review the following slides from Module 1.0 if you don't remember how to code a motor to spin based off controller input. Go to Section 3 if you remember.

Coding Motors!

Now that we've defined our electronics, let's get a motor spinning!

We'll be typing in the usercontrol() function under the while loop.

The while loop will constantly update your robot's electronics.

We're going to add an if statement to move a motor when an input (eg. if we tilt a joystick) is true.

if (controller input){
    motor spin!
}

Finding Positions of Joysticks

What's the controller input? Your joystick!

We want to see if an axis of the joystick is tilted. For this, we need to find its position. We're going to use the .position() method to help us:

.position() syntax/parameters:

(Controller name).(Axis #).position()

Axis Numbers:

  • X-axis right joystick = Axis 1
  • Y-axis right joystick = Axis 2
  • Y-axis left joystick = Axis 3
  • X-axis left joystick = Axis 4

In your program, write the following as your controller input:

Controller1.Axis1.position() > 0

This grabs the position of the X-axis right joystick.

End Result

It should end up like this:

If the Axis 1 position is greater than position 0 (tilted to the right), the motor leftWheel will spin forward.

Section 3: Coding Your Drivebase

Choosing Axes to Control Robot

We will be using an Arcade Drive control: left joystick to rotate, right joystick to move front/back

  • Axis4 (left joystick x-axis) = left/right
    If Axis4's position is negative (tilting the joystick left), you want to turn your robot left. If Axis4's position is positive (tilting the joystick right), you want to turn your robot right.
  • Axis1 (right joystick y-axis) = forward/backwards
    If Axis1's position is negative (tilting the joystick down), you want to move your robot backwards. If Axis1's position is positive (tilting the joystick up), you want to move your robot forward.

Motor Rotate Code

if (Controller1.Axis1.position() > 0){
    motor spin!
}

It's also important to note that the position values follow a coordinate plane.

On the left/right axis, all the way left = -1, all the way right = 1. All the way down = -1, all the way up = 1.

(Motor name).spin(direction)

Direction is either forward or reverse.

So, for example, you may write the following:

leftWheel.spin(forward);

Moving your Drivebase Forward

You will use Axis 1 to move your robot forward. If the position of Axis 1 is positive, then move it forward.

To move your robot forward, consider what direction each motor will rotate:

  • frontLeft = forward (use left motor group to spin forward)
  • backLeft = forward
  • frontRight = forward (use right motor group to spin forward)
  • backRight = forward

The condition for your if statement will check whether the Axis 1 position is positive. The action will be spinning all wheels forward.

Moving your Drivebase Backward

You will use Axis 1 to move your robot backward. If the position of Axis 1 is negative, then move it backward.

To move your robot backward, consider what direction each motor will rotate:

  • frontLeft = backward (use left motor group to spin backward)
  • backLeft = backward
  • frontRight = backward (use right motor group to spin backward)
  • backRight = backward

The condition for your if statement will check whether the Axis 1 position is negative. The action will be spinning all wheels backward.

Turning your Drivebase Left

You will use Axis 4 to turn your robot. If the position of Axis 4 is negative, then turn it left.

To turn your robot left, consider what direction each motor will rotate:

  • frontLeft = backward (use left motor group to spin backward)
  • backLeft = backward
  • frontRight = forward (use right motor group to spin forward)
  • backRight = forward

The condition for your if statement will check whether the Axis 4 position is negative. The action will be spinning the left wheels backward and right wheels forward.

Turning your Drivebase Right

You will use Axis 4 to turn your robot. If the position of Axis 4 is positive, then turn it right.

To turn your robot right, consider what direction each motor will rotate:

  • frontLeft = forward (use left motor group to spin forward)
  • backLeft = forward
  • frontRight = backward (use right motor group to spin backward)
  • backRight = backward

The condition for your if statement will check whether the Axis 4 position is positive. The action will be spinning the left wheels forward and right wheels backward.

Full Movement Code

Here is the full movement code for you to check your work:

Warning!

If you're completely new to code and are running through this self-guided, it is a lot better to come ask Dan Honda for help regarding this section.

quiz.question: Why do you often need to reverse some drivebase motors in code?
options: Motors on opposite sides face opposite directions, so “forward” spins them opposite ways
Because reversed motors use less battery
You never need to reverse motors
quiz.explanation: Motors on one side are mounted facing the opposite way. Reversing them (reverse = true) makes both sides drive the robot in the same direction.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.1: Intermediate Drivebase Course
lessons.content:
In this module

You should've learned:

  • Everything up to 2.1, including Module 2: Coding a Drivebase

You will learn:

  • Scaling Speed while turning in Arcade Drive
  • Scaling Speed with Arcade Drive

Table of Contents

  1. Turning & Moving Together
  2. Scaling Speed with Joysticks
  3. Extras

Section 1: Turning & Moving Together

Review

In the last module, you learned how to code an Arcade Drive! Must be nice, right?

However, during the drivebase challenge, you may have had difficulties trying to turn while driving.

Why?

This is because your code will only check the first valid "if" statement and tell the motors to run accordingly.

If both of these conditions are met, the motors are only able to move forward OR in reverse. Therefore, we will definitely encounter an error.

// move forward
if (Controller1.Axis1.position() > 0){
  leftWheels.spin(forward);
  rightWheels.spin(forward);
}

// move backward
if (Controller1.Axis1.position() < 0){
  leftWheels.spin(reverse);
  rightWheels.spin(reverse);
}

// turn left
if (Controller1.Axis4.position() < 0){
  leftWheels.spin(reverse);
  rightWheels.spin(forward);
}

// turn right
if (Controller1.Axis4.position() > 0){
  leftWheels.spin(forward);
  rightWheels.spin(reverse);
}

Solution

We need to make sure one side of the drivebase moves in accordance to how much we tilt BOTH the left and right joysticks! How? We tell each side to move in accordance to both!

We can write an equation to include both values: leftJoystick ± rightJoystick

int main(void) {
    while(1) {
        // Retrieve the necessary joystick values
        int leftY = Controller1.Axis3.position(percent);
        int rightX = Controller1.Axis1.position(percent);

        // Move the left side of the robot
        motors_left.spin(vex::directionType::fwd, leftY + rightX);

        // Move the right side of the robot
        motors_right.spin(vex::directionType::fwd, leftY - rightX);
        wait(20, msec);
    }
}

Don't just copy-paste this into your code lol. The joystick values may be flipped.

Code taken from Purdue Sigbots

Why does this work?

If Left was to move up and down, and right was to move left and right, then leftJoystick ± rightJoystick works perfectly?

Think about it:

If you want to move forward and drive right, then you tilt the left joystick up 75% and the right joystick to the right 50%.

Left would be positive, right would be positive.

Left  = leftJoystick + rightJoystick > 75%
Right = leftJoystick - rightJoystick < 75%

Left moves more than right, but right still moves in the forward direction!

Section 2: Scaling Speed with Joysticks

Scaling Speed

Driving precisely can also be a hassle. Why does the drivebase move so much even if I tilt the joystick a little?

That's because your motors will spin at the same velocity even if your joystick moves 1% upwards or 100% upwards. It's often more intuitive to code it so the more you tilt the joystick, the faster it'll go!

There are many ways to do this:

  1. Linear — If you tilt the joystick 1% upward, the robot will move 1% of its max speed. 100% tilt = 100% speed.
  2. Exponential — Speed increases exponentially with joystick tilt.

Pros and Cons

Linear is intuitive and easy to understand. It can also be precise, though you have to tilt the joystick a lot if you want to turn faster.

Exponential allows you to turn quickly without changing the joystick much, but can leave you with a lack of precision when you want to move slowly.

Which is better?

Which is better? It's up to personal preference. For Dan's team last year (Tyler was the driver), we had a mix of both. Vertically, we wouldn't change much, but we made the joystick that tilted left & right to be different:

Up until 50% tilt, the robot would turn that speed. Anything beyond that, the robot would accelerate and turn much faster.

This allowed precise control at slower speeds but fast turning when it came to it.

We'll teach you the linear scale. If you want to learn exponential or incorporate it in your code, then go for it!

Linear: setVelocity() function

As seen in Module 1.0, setVelocity() is one of the functions we can use to determine the speed of motors.

If we want the robot to move slow when the joystick moves less, that means we want the velocity to be less when the joystick position is less. That means we want to use the joystick position as a parameter in the setVelocity function.

setVelocity() function

Joystick position goes from -100 to +100, and setVelocity we use in percent, meaning also from -100% to +100% speed. Use the joystick position as a parameter in the setVelocity function:

(motor).setVelocity(axisOnePosition, percent);

Example: the joystick position value is passed directly as the velocity percentage.

Section 3: Extras

Toggling

Here's a forum page that discusses toggling pretty well.

What's toggling? If you want to move a motor and want to switch it on/off instead of holding a button, you need to create a toggle switch (a boolean) that will configure such.

bool toggleEnabled = false; // two-choice toggle, so we use bool
bool buttonPressed = false; // IGNORE, logic variable

while (true){

  bool buttonA = Controller1.ButtonA.pressing();

  //////////////////////////////////////
  // Toggle Logic
  if (buttonA && !buttonPressed){
      buttonPressed = true;
      toggleEnabled = !toggleEnabled;
  }
  else if (!buttonA) buttonPressed = false;

  //////////////////////////////////////
  // Code For toggle Enabled or Disabled
  if(toggleEnabled){
    // Do another thing
  }
  else{
    // Do initial thing
  }
}

Toggling: Why

IF ButtonA is not pressed, then ButtonPressed is true.

When you press button A, the first if statement will always run, but ONCE because buttonPressed then turns true, which allows you to change a toggle boolean once (True to false or false to true). Remember, this happens because of the if-statement priority.

Then set that toggle boolean to whatever you want.

Joystick Deadzones

Sometimes, your joystick may have a non-zero reading even if your joystick isn't moving. This is a controller problem and can lead to drifting even if you aren't purposefully moving. This happens with old controllers.

We can tell the robot not to move if the joystick value is quite low.

  1. Create a deadzone variable that is constant outside of the while-loop and initialize it to the percent of the joystick value.
  2. After your controller retrieves joystick values, compare the ABSOLUTE VALUE of it to the deadzone. If the conditions don't match, tell the robot not to move.
// Deadzone of 5
const int deadzone = 5;

int main(void) {
    while(1) {
        // Retrieve the necessary joystick values
        int left = Controller1.Axis3.position(percent);
        int right = Controller1.Axis2.position(percent);

        // std::abs takes the absolute value of whatever it is called on.
        // Thus, any values in range (-5,5) are discarded as 0.
        if(std::abs(left) < deadzone) {
            left = 0;
        }
        if(std::abs(right) < deadzone) {
            right = 0;
        }
    }
}

Abs() function

Abs(int value) takes in an integer and returns its absolute value.

An absolute value is the positive integer of its normal value.

Eg. Abs(-5) = 5
Eg. Abs(5)  = 5

This ensures that the deadzone applies no matter the direction of the joystick.

Code taken from Purdue Sigbots

quiz.question: Why can't separate if-statements turn and drive at the same time in arcade drive?
options: The code only acts on the first true “if”, so it can't combine forward + turn
The controller only has one joystick
quiz.explanation: With separate ifs, only one condition wins at a time. The fix is to add the joystick values (leftJoystick ± rightJoystick) so each side blends driving and turning.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.0: Make your Autonomous!
lessons.content:
In this module

You should've learned:

  • Everything up to Module 3, including 2.1: Intermediate Drivebase Course

You will learn:

  • Auton

Table of Contents

  1. What it is, How it Works
  2. How to Code
  3. Coding Methods

Section 1: Auton — What it is; How it Works

Autonomous: What is it?

There are two match types that involve Autonomous:

  1. Head-to-Head (Standard)
  2. Autonomous Coding Skills Match

For both of these cases, there is a period of time in which you cannot manually control your robot, and it must rely SOLELY on code. Your robot is "autonomous."

For Head-to-Head, there is a 15 second autonomous period BEFORE the driver control period. Points that you earn (including Autonomous Win Points) will contribute to your total score.

The Autonomous Coding Skills is a separate match-type which is run on the side during actual competitions. This lasts 1 minute, with a single team and one robot. The first place winner for the ENTIRE competition often goes to Worlds.

Head-to-Head

Points you score will contribute to the final score in the match. Whoever scores the most points during auton will be granted an Autonomous Bonus. This is (for High Stakes) 6 extra points! (If both alliances tie, then it's 3 points each)

Points that you score during auton (like rings in goals) will also contribute to the final score, so it's basically double the value.

There are also bonus objectives that can be fulfilled during the auton, that when completed, will grant your team an Autonomous Win Point. This is a little different; this is the second basis of ranking teams and contribute to the OVERALL ranking of your team in competition.

Head-to-Head Rules

Your robot can do a lot of stuff as you would during a normal driving period, with certain restrictions set.

  • Rules of the game still apply
  • Do not cross the autonomous line

Breaking of these rules often leads to Team or Alliance Violations or the forfeit of the Autonomous Win Point to the other alliance, depending on the violation.

Autonomous Coding Skills

The Autonomous Coding Skills Match is a single-player match type that is run during competitions alongside Head-to-Head (like Driver Skills).

All teams will get up to three attempts, and there are set conditions and rules for each game. Depending on how it works, the highest placing team during Worlds-qualifying events can go to Worlds.

Your performance on Auton Skills will contribute to Tai-Points. If you want to test it, call an Officer over and allow us to judge the points.

Section 2: How to Code

Basics

There are many ways to code auton, which can vary depending on how you want to do it.

The most common way to do so is to write methods that tell your robot to perform certain actions, like on Scratch.

For example, a method like basic5Ball() might call other methods:

void basic5Ball(){
  // outtake for shen
  intakeMove(true, 1, 50);

  moveBackwards(1.5, 12);
  moveForward(1, 6);
  moveBackwards(1.5, 12);
  moveForward(1, 6);
  pistonOn();
  pistonOff();
}

And each of those methods handles the details:

void intakeMove(bool intaking, double sec, int velo){
  if (intaking){
    intake.spin(reverse, velo, percent);
  } else {
    intake.spin(forward, velo, percent);
  }
}

Sensors

You could also incorporate sensors into your auton. These are components you put on your robot that can tell different things; e.g. a color sensor, distance sensor, etc.

It can be good if you want to be more precise with your measurements and auton code (e.g. move till you are 5 inches away from a ring vs. move 10 inches and hope for the best).

To see all sensors, look at this. If you are interested in knowing more, talk to Dan.

Writing Auton Code

You should write code under the void autonomous(){} function:

void autonomous(){
  basic5Ball();
  // launcherCode();
  // defenseActivate();
}

To make things easier, you shouldn't write methods like motors.spinFor(); directly in this area, as you'll need to write that a lot if you want to spin those motors and it can be tedious to change.

Instead, we're going to teach you how to code methods that makes this easier.

Section 3: Coding Methods

Methods

Methods are basically a set of actions that you want your code to execute when you run the method. You can include parameters in your methods to give it additional functionality and specificity. For our purposes this is the structure of a method you need to know:

void name_of_method (parameter1_type parameter1_name, parameter2_type parameter2_name, ...){

    // anything you want to run

}

"void" just means you are not returning anything, don't worry about what this means for now.

Methods Example

Here is an example of what a method could look like:

void moveVertically (double velocity, double rotations){

    allMotors.setVelocity(velocity, percent);
    allMotors.spinFor(forward, rotations, turns);

}

This is how you would run it:

moveVertically(80, 3);
moveVertically(-60, 4);

This would move your robot forward at a speed of 80 for 3 rotations, then move it backwards at a speed of 60 for 4 rotations.

Create Your Own Methods

Something to note is for autonomous, it runs code sequentially, not continuously. Therefore, you need to set the rotations of your motors, then move them all at the same time using a motor group.

This is some code to get your brains thinking, do not copy this:

void mdirection(bool m1, bool m2, bool m3, bool m4){
  topleft.setReversed(m1);
  topright.setReversed(m2);
  bottomleft.setReversed(m3);
  bottomright.setReversed(m4);
}

You can almost do anything in autonomous, get creative!

quiz.question: In a standard Head-to-Head match, how long is the autonomous period?
quiz.explanation: Head-to-Head matches have a 15-second autonomous period before driver control. (The separate Autonomous Coding Skills match runs for 1 minute.)

lessons.title: Lesson 4.0: PID (Theory)
lessons.content:
In this module

You should've learned:

  • Everything up to Module 4, including Lesson 3.0: Make your Autonomous

You will learn:

  • Why simple "move for X seconds" autons aren't precise
  • What a control loop is
  • The three parts of a PID controller: Proportional, Integral, and Derivative

Heads up: this lesson is theory only — there's no code yet. We'll write real PID code in Lesson 4.1. Understanding the why first will make the code make a lot more sense.

Recap: How we've coded auton so far

Last time, we taught auton using methods like moveForward(1, 6). This is useful and it works!

However, the way we taught you was very beginner-like:

  • Pros: It works.
  • Cons: It's not precise.

How can we improve?

Most teams code their robot like:

  • Move motor for X seconds / rotations

This isn't bad, but it isn't precise. Why?

  • Motors running on time/rotations won't always run the same every time.
  • Heating, battery level, and inconsistent wear & tear all change how far the robot actually goes.

It's generally better to code based on distance:

  • Move motor for X inches — and keep checking until you actually get there.

That idea — "keep checking how far off you are and correct yourself" — is exactly what a PID controller does.

Control Variables

Every control problem has the same basic pieces. The thing you're trying to control is called the plant (for us, that's usually the motors / drivebase).

  • Input (actuating signal): the command we send in — e.g. motor power.
  • Plant: the system we want to control (the motors).
  • Output (controlled variable): what actually happens — e.g. the robot's position.

The big question: how do we generate the right input so we get the output we want?

The Feedback Loop

The trick is to feed the output back and compare it to what we wanted. The difference between them is called the error.

  • Commanded variable: what we want the system to do (the target / setpoint).
  • Error term: commanded value − actual value. We want this to be zero.
  • Controller: the part we design. Its job is to drive the error to zero over time.
  • Feedback path: we constantly measure the output and loop it back to recalculate the error.

This whole lesson is about designing that controller in the middle.

An Example: a hovering drone

PID is easiest to picture with a flying drone. Say we want the drone to fly up and hover at 50 meters.

The drone starts on the ground (altitude = 0). Our target is 50 meters, so right now:

error = target - actual = 50 - 0 = 50

Part 1: Proportional control

The simplest controller just multiplies the error by a number. Let's call that number the controller (also called the gain):

Propeller Speed = Error × Controller

This is the Proportional term. The further you are from the target, the harder you push. As you get close, error shrinks, so you ease off.

What can we control?

We can't change the error directly — that depends on where the drone actually is. The one thing we get to pick is the controller (gain). Say we pick 0.1:

  • At altitude = 0 → error = 50 → Propeller Speed = 50 × 0.1 = 5
  • At altitude = 30 → error = 20 → Propeller Speed = 20 × 0.1 = 2

Notice the propeller slows down as the drone rises. That's the proportional behavior.

What happens with proportional only?

Think of it like walking up to a wall: you walk fast when you're far away, and slow down as you get close.

The distance curve rises quickly then flattens out as it approaches the target. The speed curve starts high and shrinks toward zero. Looks great… but there's a hidden problem.

The Problem: steady-state error

Let's say the drone needs 100 rpm just to hover (to fight gravity). Now suppose our controller is 5:

Propeller Speed = Error × Controller
100 rpm needed to hover
=> Error × 5 = 100
=> Error = 20

The drone would hover at 30 meters (error of 20 below the 50m target) and just… stay there. It never reaches the goal!

Why can't we just turn up the gain?

You might think: "just make the controller bigger." But look at what happens — the error never actually disappears, it just gets smaller:

Error × Gain = Propeller Speed
  50  ×   2  =  100 rpm
  20  ×   5  =  100 rpm
  10  ×  10  =  100 rpm
   1  × 100  =  100 rpm   ← error still isn't zero!

No matter how big the gain is, you always need some leftover error to produce the 100 rpm needed to hover. This leftover gap is called steady-state error.

So how do we get rid of it?

Part 2: the Integral (using the past)

The fix is to give the controller a memory. The Integral term keeps a running total of all the error over time.

Think of the integral as the area under the error curve — it adds up every little bit of error, tick after tick.

As long as any error remains, the integral keeps growing — which keeps adding more and more power until the error is finally gone.

Proportional + Integral working together

Propeller Speed = Proportional + Integral
  • Far from target: Proportional is high (and shrinking), Integral is low (and rising fast).
  • Near the target: Proportional is low, Integral is high — and it's the integral that finishes the job.

The result

Now the drone climbs all the way to 50 meters with zero error. The steady-state error is gone. This works!

The next problem: overshoot

A proportional + integral (PI) loop works, but the path it takes might not be ideal. Because the integral has built up a big total, it can carry the drone past the target before settling back.

That's called overshoot — the drone blows past 50m, then has to come back down. For a robot, overshoot means slamming past your target and wobbling back. Not great.

Part 3: the Derivative (predicting the future)

The last term watches how fast the error is changing. The Derivative term looks at the rate of change and applies the brakes before we overshoot.

  • It looks at the rate of change of the error.
  • If we're approaching the target very fast, the derivative produces a negative value that slows us down early.
  • In short: it prematurely slows you down so you ease into the target instead of crashing through it.

That's why we say: Integral = the past, Proportional = the present, Derivative = the future.

Putting it all together: PID

Add all three terms together, each with its own weighting factor (a constant we tune): kP, kI, and kD.

output = (kP × Proportional) + (kI × Integral) + (kD × Derivative)
TermLooks atJob
P — Proportional (kP)The present errorPush harder the further you are from the target
I — Integral (kI)The past (sum of error)Erase leftover steady-state error
D — Derivative (kD)The future (rate of change)Slow down early to prevent overshoot

Those three weighting factors (kP, kI, kD) are the numbers you tune to make your robot move smoothly and accurately.

Up next

That's the theory! In Lesson 4.1: Tasks & PID (Implementation), we'll turn this into real VEX C++ code — using a task so the PID loop runs in the background while your auton tells it where to go.

Questions?

PID is one of the trickier concepts in VEX. If any of this felt fuzzy, that's totally normal — come ask Dan Honda to walk through it with you before moving on to the code.

quiz.question: What do the three letters in a PID controller stand for?
quiz.explanation: PID = Proportional, Integral, Derivative. Together they correct the robot's error smoothly and precisely instead of just moving for a fixed time.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.1: Tasks & PID (Implementation)
lessons.content:
In this module

You should've learned:

  • Everything up to Lesson 4.1, including Lesson 4.0: PID (Theory)

You will learn:

  • What a task is and how to make one
  • How to turn the PID theory into real VEX C++ code
  • How to run your PID loop in the background during auton

This lesson builds directly on the theory from 4.0. If you don't remember what P, I, and D do, go back and review first!

Tasks: Definition

A task is an "independent thread of execution."

In plain English: tasks are a way to run multiple things simultaneously, with code that constantly updates and keeps running on its own.

Examples of tasks you might use:

  • Printing information on the brain
  • Tracking the position of the robot
  • PID
  • A main method that runs your whole match

Why do we need a task for PID? Because PID has to recalculate over and over, forever, while the rest of your auton keeps making decisions. A task lets the PID math run in the background while your auton just says "go to this position."

Tasks: Important Information

  • Tasks run independently but can use global variables (unlike normal methods). This is how we'll communicate with our PID loop — the auton changes a global variable, and the task reacts to it.
  • Task limit: 20. You can't have more than 20 running at once.
  • Tasks run on a priority system. You can give each task a priority level; higher-priority tasks get more CPU time and run ahead of lower-priority ones.

Warning: Task priority is complicated and can cause a lot of hard-to-find errors if you don't understand it. A common misconception is that equal-priority tasks each get the same amount of time to run — that's not guaranteed. For now, stick to the basics below.

How we'll run tasks in PID

Here's the overall plan, in pseudocode:

auton() {
    Start PID task

    Change global variables that tell PID where to move
    (wait for PID to move)

    Change global variables that tell PID where to move next
    etc...

    End PID task
}

The key idea: tasks should only run when we want them to. Start the PID task at the beginning of auton, feed it target positions, and stop it when you're done.

How to make a task

A task looks a lot like a method! Two differences: it returns an int, and it contains a while loop so it keeps running.

int nameOfTask() {        // task is just a function that returns an int

    { insert setup code here }

    while (1) {            // while loop keeps the task running forever
        { insert code here }

        vex::task::sleep(20);   // keeps the CPU safe (don't hog it!)
    }

    return 0;              // return value for the int
}
  • The while (1) loop is what makes a task keep running.
  • vex::task::sleep(20); pauses the loop for 20 milliseconds each cycle so you don't overload the CPU. Never leave this out.
  • return 0; at the end satisfies the int return type.

The PID Task

Now let's build the PID loop itself. Remember the full controller from Lesson 4.0 — kP, kI, kD weighting the Proportional (present), Integral (past), and Derivative (future) terms:

Pseudocode for the task:

1. Set kP, kI, kD variables
2. LOOP:
     a. Get current position
     b. Calculate the PID values
     c. Make the drivebase move based on the output
     d. Repeat

Step 1: Set up your variables

At the top of your program (as global variables, so the task can see them), define your tuning constants and the working variables for both lateral (forward/back) and turning movement:

// settings (the constants you'll tune)
double kP = 0.1;
double kI = 0.0;
double kD = 0.0;

double turnkP = 0.0;
double turnkI = 0.0;
double turnkD = 0.0;

// lateral (forward/backward) PID working variables
int error;          // sensorValue - desiredValue : how far off we are
int prevError = 0;  // the error from 20 ms ago
int totalError;     // totalError = totalError + error : the integral
int derivative;     // error - prevError : the rate of change

// turning PID working variables
int turnError;
int turnPrevError = 0;
int turnTotalError;
int turnDerivative;

// auton settings (these are what your auton will change)
int desiredValue = 0;
int desiredTurnValue = 0;

bool resetDriveSensors = false;
bool enableDrivePID = false;   // master on/off switch for the task

Notice how each working variable maps to a PID term: error = Proportional, totalError = Integral, derivative = Derivative.

Step 2: Get the current position

Inside the task's loop, read how far the wheels have turned. We average the left and right motor positions to get one overall position:

// average of the two sides
int leftMotorPosition = LeftMotors.position(degrees);
int rightMotorPosition = RightMotors.position(degrees);
int averagePosition = -(leftMotorPosition + rightMotorPosition) / 2;

Tip: you could also use an inertial sensor for the position/heading instead of motor encoders — it's often more accurate for turns.

Step 3: Calculate the lateral PID

This is the theory turned into code. Compare the three terms below to the diagram above:

error = averagePosition - desiredValue;   // P : present error

derivative = error - prevError;           // D : rate of change

// I : running total (Velocity -> Position -> Absement)
totalError += error;

double lateralMotorPower = (error * kP) + (derivative * kD) + (totalError * kI);

At the end of the loop, remember to save the current error for next time and sleep:

prevError = error;
vex::task::sleep(20);

Step 3.5: Calculate the turning PID

Turning works exactly the same way, but instead of the average of the two sides we use the difference between them (that tells us how much the robot has rotated):

///////////////////
// Turning Movement PID
///////////////////

// difference of the two sides tells us how far we've turned
int turnDifference = leftMotorPosition - rightMotorPosition;

turnError = turnDifference - desiredTurnValue;

turnDerivative = turnError - turnPrevError;

turnTotalError += turnError;

double turnMotorPower = (turnError * turnkP) + (turnDerivative * turnkD) + (turnTotalError * turnkI);

And, like before, save the previous turn error: turnPrevError = turnError;

Step 4: Move the drivebase

Finally, combine the lateral and turning power and send it to the motors. Adding the turn power to one side and subtracting it from the other is what makes the robot drive straight and turn at the same time:

LeftMotors.spin(forward,  lateralMotorPower + turnMotorPower, voltageUnits::volt);
RightMotors.spin(forward, lateralMotorPower - turnMotorPower, voltageUnits::volt);

That's the entire PID task — Steps 2 through 4 all live inside the while loop from earlier so they repeat forever.

How to use your task

Once the task function (let's call it drivePID) is written, here's how you control it from your auton:

Start the task:

vex::task PIDmodifier(drivePID);

Stop the task:

PIDmodifier.stop();

Tell it where to go (just change the global variables):

resetDriveSensors = true;
desiredValue = -240;     // drive to this position
desiredTurnValue = 0;    // and this heading

The full auton

Putting it all together, a simple auton that drives the robot one move looks like this:

void auton() {
    // the task runs in the background during auton (or driver control)

    enableDrivePID = true;
    vex::task PIDmodifier(drivePID);

    resetDriveSensors = true;
    desiredValue = -240;
    desiredTurnValue = 0;

    vex::task::sleep(1000);   // give the robot time to actually get there

    enableDrivePID = false;
    PIDmodifier.stop();
}

To add more movements, just change desiredValue / desiredTurnValue again and add another sleep() before stopping the task.

Bonus: print to make your life easier

While tuning, it's super helpful to print your live values to the controller screen so you can see what PID is doing:

Controller1.Screen.setCursor(1, 1);
Controller1.Screen.print(desiredValue);
Controller1.Screen.setCursor(2, 1);
Controller1.Screen.print(averagePosition);
Controller1.Screen.setCursor(3, 1);
Controller1.Screen.print(error);

Watching error shrink toward zero on the screen tells you your PID is working — and helps you tune kP, kI, and kD.

Warning!

Tasks and PID are genuinely advanced topics. If you're running through this self-guided and something breaks (especially around task priority or tuning), come ask Dan Honda for help rather than guessing.

quiz.question: What is a “task” in VEX programming?
options: An independent thread that runs code continuously in the background
quiz.explanation: A task is an independent thread of execution — it lets PID math recalculate over and over in the background while the rest of your auton keeps making decisions.

lessons.title: Lesson 4.2: Tune tune tune!
lessons.content:
A tip for making a good auton…

It starts with a t, ends with an e, and rhymes with goon?

… Tune! 🎵

That's the whole secret of this lesson. Write it on your hand. Tune, tune, tune.

In this module

You should've learned:

  • Everything up to Lesson 4.2, including Lesson 4.1: Tasks & PID (Implementation)

You will learn:

  • Why tuning is the most important step in a good auton
  • How to tune your movement distances (forward/back and turning)
  • The full PID tuning process
  • A simpler PD tuning process that many teams actually use

Why tuning matters

You can write a perfect PID task and your robot will still drive into a wall if the numbers aren't tuned. A great auton isn't about fancy code — it's about patiently dialing in the values until the robot hits the same spot every single time.

There is no magic number you can copy from another team. Every robot is different: weight, gear ratio, wheel size, and even battery level all change how it moves. The only way to find your numbers is to… you guessed it. Tune, tune, tune.

The whole process is the same loop every time: change a number → test → watch what happens → change it again.

Part 1: Tuning your distances (forward/back & turning)

This is the easy part. Remember the two global variables from Lesson 4.1:

  • desiredValue — how far to drive forward/backward
  • desiredTurnValue — how far to turn

To change how far your robot goes, you just change the numerical value and test. That's it.

resetDriveSensors = true;
desiredValue = -240;     // ← change this number to change the distance
desiredTurnValue = 0;    // ← change this number to change the turn
  • Want it to drive further? Make the number bigger.
  • Want it to drive backward? Make the number negative.
  • Turning works exactly the same way — just change desiredTurnValue.

The process: these values are in motor degrees, not inches, so you can't just type the distance you want. Instead: pick a number, run it, measure how far the robot actually went, then nudge the number up or down and run it again. Repeat until it lands exactly where you want.

Pro tip: Once you find that, say, 240 degrees = 12 inches on your robot, write it down! Now you can reuse that ratio to estimate any distance instead of guessing from scratch every time.

Part 2: Tuning the PID constants

This is the real tuning — getting your robot to move smoothly and accurately instead of jerking around. You're adjusting the three constants from Lesson 4.1:

  • kP — push proportional to how far off you are
  • kI — erase leftover error so you don't stop short
  • kD — slow down early to prevent overshoot

Two rules before you start:

  1. Change only ONE constant at a time. If you change two and it improves, you won't know which one helped.
  2. Tune lateral and turning separately. Tune your forward/back PID first (set desiredTurnValue = 0), then tune your turning PID (set desiredValue = 0).

The PID tuning process (order matters!)

  1. Start with everything at 0. Set kP = 0, kI = 0, kD = 0.
  2. Tune kP first. Slowly raise kP and test after each change.
    • Too low → robot is sluggish and stops short of the target.
    • Too high → robot overshoots and oscillates (wobbles back and forth past the target).
    • Goal: reaches the target quickly with just a small overshoot/wobble. Don't try to make it perfect yet — that's kD's job.
  3. Tune kD next. Slowly raise kD to dampen that wobble.
    • Too low → still wobbles before settling.
    • Too high → movement gets jerky or stutters.
    • Goal: the robot glides smoothly to a stop with no wobble.
  4. Tune kI last — and keep it tiny. Only touch this if the robot consistently stops a little short of the target every time.
    • Raise kI in very small steps.
    • Too much → the error "winds up" and the robot overshoots and slowly oscillates. This is a classic trap, so be gentle.
    • Many teams leave kI at 0 entirely (see the PD section below).

Troubleshooting cheat sheet

What you seeWhat to change
Overshoots / wobbles past the targetLower kP or raise kD
Too slow / stops shortRaise kP
Wobbles back and forth foreverRaise kD
Movement is jerky / stuttersLower kD
Stops just short every single timeAdd a tiny bit of kI

Tip: print error to the controller screen (from Lesson 4.1) while you tune — watching it shrink to zero tells you it's working.

The PD tuning process (the simpler one)

Here's a secret: a lot of VEX teams skip the I term completely and just use PD (Proportional + Derivative).

Why? The integral term is the trickiest to tune and is the one most likely to cause overshoot (windup). A well-tuned PD loop is simpler, very stable, and more than good enough for most autons — you only have two numbers to worry about instead of three.

The PD process

  1. Leave kI = 0 and don't touch it.
  2. Tune kP until the robot reaches the target quickly with a slight overshoot.
  3. Tune kD until that overshoot is gone and the robot settles smoothly.

Done! Two numbers, stable robot.

When should you go back to full PID? Only if your robot reliably stops a tiny bit short of the target and raising kP can't fix it without causing wobble. That leftover gap (steady-state error from Lesson 4.0) is exactly what the I term is for — so add a small kI and you're back to full PID.

Tuning tips to live by

  • Change one number at a time.
  • Make small changes — tuning is about nudging, not jumping.
  • Test on the real field you'll compete on (carpet vs. foam tiles totally changes the feel).
  • Tune lateral and turning separately.
  • Write down your good values so you never lose them.
  • Be patient. Good auton takes real time — budget for it.

tune tune tune

There's no shortcut and no copy-paste answer. The teams with the best autons aren't the ones with the fanciest code — they're the ones who sat down and tuned, tuned, tuned until it was perfect.

Warning!

Tuning can be frustrating, and it's easy to chase your tail changing numbers randomly. If you've been at it a while and it still isn't behaving, come grab Dan Honda — a second set of eyes on your robot's behavior usually spots the problem fast.

quiz.question: What's the one-word secret to a good autonomous, according to this lesson?
quiz.explanation: Tune, tune, tune! Even perfect PID code drives into a wall if the numbers aren't tuned. Every robot is different, so you patiently dial in the values.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.0: Making Objects
lessons.content:
In this module

You should've learned:

  • How to set up your environment for the Advanced course (PROS + LemLib). If you haven't installed LemLib yet, go back to Setting up your environment (Advanced).

You will learn:

  • What objects are and how to make them
  • How to declare your motors, controllers, and sensors
  • Why a negative port number reverses a motor
  • How easy odometry is to set up with LemLib

Welcome to the Advanced Course!

The Advanced course uses PROS with the LemLib library instead of VEXcode. PROS gives you more power and control, and LemLib does the hard math (PID, odometry, motion) for you. Before anything works, your robot needs to know what hardware it has — and that's done by making objects.

What is an object?

An object is a variable that represents a real thing on your robot — a motor, the controller, a sensor, a piston. Just like you made int or bool variables in the beginner course, here you make a Motor, a Controller, or an Imu.

The general pattern looks like this:

(type) (yourName)(parameters);

For example, a controller object named tylerC:

pros::Controller tylerC(pros::E_CONTROLLER_MASTER);

The type (pros::Controller) says what kind of thing it is. The name (tylerC) is whatever you want to call it. The parameters in the brackets are the settings — here, which controller it is.

📖 Use the official LemLib docs as you go. They show you exactly how to declare each variable, with full examples:
lemlib.readthedocs.io — Configuration Tutorial

Step 1: Plug your motors in

Before you write a single line of code, physically plug your motors into the brain and note which port each one uses. The port number on the brain has to match the port number in your code — if your left motor is plugged into port 11, then port 11 goes in the code for that motor.

Change the port number of each object to match what's actually plugged in. This is the #1 thing beginners get wrong: the code looks perfect, but the motor doesn't move because it's looking at the wrong port.

Step 2: Make your motor objects

A single motor object looks like this:

pros::Motor intakeFlip(5, pros::MotorGearset::green);

That makes a motor named intakeFlip on port 5, using a green (200 RPM) gear cartridge. Match the gearset to your motor's cartridge color:

CartridgeGearsetSpeed
Redpros::MotorGearset::red100 RPM (most torque)
Greenpros::MotorGearset::green200 RPM
Bluepros::MotorGearset::blue600 RPM (fastest)

Motor groups

Your drivebase has several motors per side that always spin together. Instead of one object each, bundle them into a motor group by listing all the ports in { }:

// Left side of the drivebase - ports 11, 8, 6
pros::MotorGroup leftMotors({-11, -8, -6}, pros::MotorGearset::blue);
// Right side of the drivebase - ports 17, 20, 9
pros::MotorGroup rightMotors({17, 20, 9}, pros::MotorGearset::blue);

Step 3: Negative port = reversed motor ⚠️

Look closely at the left motors above — the ports are negative (-11, -8, -6). That's not a typo!

Putting a minus sign in front of the port number flips the direction that motor spins. One side of your drivebase faces the opposite way from the other, so its motors have to spin the opposite direction for the robot to drive straight.

So when you make your objects:

  • If a motor spins the wrong way, make its port number negative (e.g. change 11 to -11).
  • If it's already going the right way, leave it positive.

This is how you adjust each motor to spin the way you need it to — no rewiring required, just a minus sign.

Putting it all together

Here's a real, full set of objects from a competition robot — controllers, drivebase motor groups, intake motors, an inertial sensor, an optical sensor, and pneumatic pistons. This is what your declarations look like all in one place (this is just an example — your ports and names will be different):

// Controllers
pros::Controller tylerC(pros::E_CONTROLLER_MASTER);
pros::Controller tokumaC(pros::E_CONTROLLER_PARTNER);

// Motor groups
// Left motor group - ports 11, 8, 6 (reversed)
pros::MotorGroup leftMotors({-11, -8, -6}, pros::MotorGearset::blue);
// Right motor group - ports 17, 20, 9
pros::MotorGroup rightMotors({17, 20, 9}, pros::MotorGearset::blue);

// Intake motor group - port 12 (11W) and port 10 (5.5W)
pros::MotorGroup intake({-12, -10}, pros::MotorGearset::blue);
// Individual control for port 12 (11W motor)
pros::Motor intakeBottom(-12, pros::MotorGearset::blue);
// Individual control for port 10 (5.5W motor - slows down when a block is detected)
pros::Motor intakeTop(-10, pros::MotorGearset::green);
// 5.5W intake motor on port 5 (green = 200 RPM)
pros::Motor intakeFlip(5, pros::MotorGearset::green);

// Inertial (IMU) sensor on port 7
pros::Imu imu(7);

// Optical sensor on port 18
pros::Optical opt(18);

// Pneumatics (pistons)
pros::adi::Pneumatics hood('C', false);    // Hood - lifts up when scoring (R1+R2)
pros::adi::Pneumatics tongue('B', false);  // Tongue mechanism
pros::adi::Pneumatics wing('A', false);    // Wing

And here's how it looks inside the editor — notice the faint labels (id:, gearset:, port:) that VS Code shows you to remind you what each parameter does:

Sensors and pistons follow the exact same pattern as motors: a type, a name, and the port (or ADI port letter) it's plugged into.

Odometry is easy with LemLib

Odometry is how your robot tracks its own position (X, Y, heading) on the field in real time — it's what makes accurate autonomous routes possible. Coding this from scratch would be a nightmare of math… but with LemLib, odometry is genuinely easy. You just make a few more objects.

You bundle your tracking wheels and inertial sensor into one OdomSensors object. You pass in the things you have, and write nullptr ("nothing here") for the ones you don't:

// sensors for odometry
lemlib::OdomSensors sensors(&vertical,    // vertical tracking wheel
                            nullptr,      // vertical tracking wheel 2
                            &horizontal,  // horizontal tracking wheel
                            nullptr,      // horizontal tracking wheel 2
                            &imu          // inertial sensor
);

That's it — LemLib takes those objects and handles all the position-tracking math for you. The & in front of &vertical and &imu just means "the object I made earlier." Because you already practiced making objects above, setting up odometry is just making a few more objects and handing them to LemLib.

📖 For the full configuration (tracking wheels, the drivetrain, and the chassis), follow along with the official tutorial:
lemlib.readthedocs.io — Configuration Tutorial

Recap

  • An object represents a real device: type name(parameters);
  • Plug in your motors and set each object's port number to match the brain.
  • A negative port number reverses the motor — use it to make each side spin the right way.
  • Match the gearset to your cartridge color (red / green / blue).
  • Odometry is easy with LemLib — it's just a few more objects.
  • When in doubt, the LemLib docs show you exactly how to declare everything.

quiz.question: What happens if you put a negative sign in front of a motor's port number (e.g. -11)?
options: It reverses the direction that motor spins
quiz.explanation: A negative port number flips the motor's spin direction — handy for making one side of the drivebase match the other without rewiring.
